content: Capacitors are utilized to detect changes in acceleration, such as when functioning as tilt sensors or in applications like free-fall detection, where they can trigger airbag deployment. They are also employed in various other applications. Certain fingerprint sensors operate using capacitors. Additionally, in a theremin musical instrument, the pitch can be adjusted by moving the hand, as this alters the effective capacitance between the user’s hand and the antenna. Capacitive touch switches work by changing the effective area of the plates. In pulsed power and weapons systems, large, specially designed, low-inductance, high-voltage capacitors (known as capacitor banks) are used to deliver massive pulses of current for numerous applications. These include electromagnetic forming, Marx generators, pulsed lasers (especially TEA lasers), pulse-forming networks, radar systems, fusion research, and particle accelerators. Large capacitor banks also serve as energy sources for exploding-bridgewire detonators or slapper detonators in nuclear weapons and other specialized weaponry. Experimental research is ongoing to use capacitor banks as power sources for electromagnetic armor, railguns, and coilguns. Explosively pumped flux compression generators are also related to these applications. Capacitors can retain an electrical charge long after power is removed from a circuit, posing risks of electric shocks (potentially fatal) or damage to connected equipment. For example, a 5-volt AA battery contains a capacitor that can be charged to over 300 volts, capable of delivering a highly painful shock. It is crucial to ensure that any large or high-voltage capacitor is properly discharged before servicing the equipment containing it. For board-level capacitors, this is achieved by placing a bleeder resistor across the terminals. The resistor’s value is chosen to be high enough to avoid affecting the circuit but low enough to discharge the capacitor shortly after power is removed. High-voltage capacitors should be stored with their terminals shorted, as temporarily discharged capacitors can develop dangerous voltages if left open-circuited. Large, oil-filled capacitors from older designs must be disposed of properly, as some contain polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs). PCBs are known carcinogens and can contaminate groundwater if improperly discarded. Modern electrical components no longer use PCBs, but older capacitors labeled with trade names like Askarel may still contain them. High-voltage capacitors present unique hazards beyond the usual risks associated with high-voltage, high-energy circuits. These capacitors can fail catastrophically when subjected to voltages or currents beyond their ratings or as they reach the end of their operational life. Failures in the dielectric or metal interconnections can lead to arcing (arc faults), especially in oil-filled units, which may vaporize the dielectric fluid. This can result in case bulging, rupture, or even explosions that disperse flammable oil, start fires, and damage nearby equipment. Cylindrical glass or plastic cases are more prone to explosive rupture than rectangular cases due to their inability to expand under pressure. Capacitors used in RF or sustained high-current applications can overheat, particularly in the center of the capacitor rolls, leading to rapid internal heating and destruction, even if the outer case remains relatively cool. In high-energy capacitor banks, a fault in one capacitor can cause a sudden release of energy stored in the rest of the bank, leading to violent explosions. High-voltage vacuum capacitors can also generate soft X-rays during normal operation. To mitigate these risks, proper containment, fusing, and preventative maintenance are essential. High-voltage capacitors can benefit from pre-charging to limit inrush currents during the power-up of HVDC circuits. This practice extends the component’s lifespan and reduces high-voltage hazards.
